name: PT Bank Mestika Dharma Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bank Mestika Dharma: a thin float carrying a price the returns cannot justify
frontmatter.summary: Bank Mestika trades at 9.4 times today's fundamental value of Rp217, nearly nine times the Rp231 twelve-month value, because a 9.1% free float on a flagged concentrated-ownership name clears at scarcity prices, not because it earns its cost of capital. ROE of 5.1% against a 12.5% COE warrants a P/B far below the traded multiple. SELL, target Rp1,137.
thesis: The franchise does not earn its cost of capital: FY2026E ROE of 5.1% against an 12.5% COE builds a warranted P/B of 0.30 times, and the primary method already carries half the weight [S7][S0].
The traded multiple of 1.45 times book and 29.2x earnings is a float price: 9.1% free float, high-shareholding-concentration status and a traded value below the fund's liquidity floor [S0][S9].
The free-float rule forces a step to 12.5% by 31 March 2027, a 3.4% supply gap that is a sell-down or an issue, not a demand event [S11][S0].

The base case is a slow bank, not a broken one: NIM 5.6%, credit cost 0.4% and cost-to-income 60.0% reproduce the FY2025 economics, and KBMI II is reached from retained earnings without a rights issue [S6][S8].
The konglo lens, not a bearish forecast, sets the target: the base regime case keeps 40% of the log gap and values the shares at Rp884, the bear regime case at Rp361 [S0][S12].

catalysts.event: Free float must reach the intermediate regulatory threshold
MSCI consultation feedback window on Standalone status closes
Final free-float deadline under the exchange rule
Management's target date for the KBMI II core-capital threshold

blocks.text: We initiate Bank Mestika Dharma at **SELL** with a twelve-month target of Rp1,137, a total return of -43.1% from a price of Rp2,030. The call is not a bet against the bank's solvency or its deposit franchise: it is a statement that the price is a float price and that the fundamentals that would have to support it are not there. Our fundamental twelve-month value, after an explicit 30% liquidity discount for a name that trades a few million rupiah a day, is Rp231 a share; the price sits at 9.4 times today's value of Rp217 and at just under nine times that twelve-month figure [S0]. The konglo lens then does what the house card says it must: it does not pretend the gap closes in a year. The base regime case keeps 40% of the log gap and gives Rp884; the probability-weighted target across the regime scenarios is the Rp1,137 we publish.

The variant view is simple and uncomfortable. A reader who looks only at the dividend sees a yield of 1.0%; a reader who looks only at book sees 1.45 times it. Neither is the point. The point is that the bank earns 5.1% on equity against a 12.5% cost of capital, so every rupiah of retained book is worth well under a rupiah, and the multiple is held up by the fact that 9.1% of the shares are available to trade while the controller owns the rest [S0][S9]. That is a regime variable, not a fundamental one, and the 2026 regime has started to price it.

What moves the value, in order: the margin and the cost base, which the sensitivity grid runs both ways around the base case; the credit charge, where the market currently assumes the near-zero provisioning of FY2024 and FY2025 continues; and the capital path, because a rights issue to reach KBMI II would dilute book per share just as returns stay below the cost of equity [S8]. The upside risk to our call is a control or consolidation transaction: it is a real path once the KBMI tier disappears, but at today's multiple an acquirer would be paying far above what the franchise returns justify, which is why it is in the signposts and the valuation does not carry it.

Bank Mestika Dharma is a small Indonesian commercial bank headquartered in Medan, North Sumatra, incorporated in 1955 and listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange; it is a subsidiary of PT Mestika Benua Mas, and the controlling shareholder group holds the overwhelming majority of the shares [S0]. It takes savings, current and time deposits and lends against them: multi-purpose and working-capital credit, mortgages, car and land loans, trade finance and investment credit, alongside mobile and internet banking, remittance, foreign exchange, tax payment and bancassurance services [S0]. There is no insurance arm, no multifinance subsidiary and no securities business in the model: this is a single-engine deposit-and-lend franchise.

The shape of the balance sheet is the first thing to understand about it. Loans are about two thirds of total assets [S6]; the rest is largely government securities, placements and central-bank balances, which is why the bank reports a capital adequacy ratio of 46.5% [S7]. Deposits of IDR10,990.0bn fund loans of IDR11,060.0bn, a loan-to-deposit ratio of 1.0x [S6][S0]: the bank is fully lent against its deposit base and has no wholesale funding cushion to speak of. That combination — a fully lent book, a securities portfolio, and capital at roughly twice what the risk assets require — is the economic signature of the whole thesis.

The distribution footprint is regional and small: one operational head office, 14 branch offices, thirty-nine sub-branches, further cash-service sub-branches and cash-recycling machines across the ATM Bersama network [S7]. Management opened a branch in Semarang in 2025, arguing that Central Java's export manufacturing and relatively competitive regional wages made it the right second province; the stated logic was to follow existing customers who were expanding there [S7]. That is a plausible growth story and an expensive one: the cost base carries the new branch before the revenue does, which is exactly what the H1-2026 numbers show [S0][S7].

Strategy is therefore narrow and explicit. The five-year corporate plan for 2024-2028 is built around raising core capital to the KBMI II threshold of IDR6.00tn before the end of 2028, organically, from retained earnings and balance-sheet growth rather than from an equity issue [S8]. Management told the exchange that core capital rose from IDR5.09tn at the end of 2024 to IDR5.35tn by September 2025 and that it expects to meet the timetable [S8]. The gap is small in absolute terms; closing it is a matter of not paying out too much, which is why the payout ratio matters more here than the loan growth rate.

Competitively the bank is a challenger, not a leader. In Medan it competes with the state banks, the large private banks and the regional development banks; nationally it is a rounding error in system loans. Its edge, to the extent it has one, is relationships in a specific commercial community and a deposit franchise that has repriced slowly — the same franchise that has kept the margin near 5.6% while the loan book grew 3.6% in FY2025 [S6][S7]. Nothing in the sources reviewed suggests pricing power: the 2025 results commentary attributes the profit decline to weaker operating income and higher costs, not to a lost client base [S6].

Indonesian commercial banking is a deposit-funded spread business supervised by the OJK, with banks sorted by core-capital size into the KBMI tiers that set supervisory intensity, and deposits guaranteed to a limit by the deposit insurance agency [S8]. The tier structure is the live regulatory fact for this name. Under the KBMI framework a bank with core capital up to IDR6.00tn sits in the lowest tier; above it, the second tier runs to a much larger capital base, and the tiers above that are occupied by the large private and state franchises [S8]. The OJK has said it intends to remove the lowest tier, which forces every bank sitting in it to choose between consolidation and a capital raise [S8]. That is the single most important industry fact in this report: it converts a sleepy regional bank into a participant in a consolidation process with a deadline.

The macro backdrop is not helpful. The house macro deck carries Bank Indonesia's policy rate flat at 5.8% through the forecast years, inflation near 3.3% and real growth of 5.3%, with the rupiah at 18,350 to the dollar against a spot of 18,039 under a balance-of-payments-pressure regime [S0]. For a bank the relevant transmission is the deposit side: when the policy rate is flat and liquidity is tight, small banks with a thin current-account franchise pay up for time deposits, and the margin compresses before the loan book reacts. That is the mechanism that took the FY2025 cost of funds higher and the net interest income lower even as loans grew [S6]. The house bank card asks for that mechanism to be quantified as a deposit beta on the policy-rate path and as a current-account/savings versus time-deposit mix, and we cannot: no archived source discloses the CASA split or a deposit beta, and the pack carries only total customer deposits [S6][S0]. We record the mix and the beta as an evidence gap rather than a clean pass and argue the squeeze from the reported cost of funds. For the same reason, the capital ratio quoted throughout is the reported total capital adequacy ratio of 46.5% [S7]: total capital includes tier-two instruments, so that ratio sits at or above the common-equity tier-one ratio, and we use it because it is what the bank discloses, while the excess-capital arithmetic in section four is done on book equity against risk-weighted assets rather than on the ratio itself. The common-equity split is recorded as an evidence gap with the deposit beta, not inferred from the total.

Regulation beyond the capital tiers cuts two ways. On one side, the exchange has raised the minimum free float and set deadlines that reach this name: issuers with a market capitalisation above the large-cap threshold and a float below the intermediate one must reach 12.5% by the end of March 2027 and the full minimum by the end of March 2028 [S11]. On the other, MSCI opened a consultation in October 2026 on reclassifying Indonesia from Emerging to Standalone status, with a freeze on index increases in place until further notice, feedback until the end of April 2027 and a decision by the end of June 2027 [S12]. Both point the same way for a stock whose price is set at the float margin: they are supply and visibility events, not earnings events.

The competitive map inside the industry is unkind to a bank of this size. Funding costs are set by the largest deposit franchises; loan pricing in SME and consumer segments is contested by the multifinance companies and by the digital banks that have spent the last several years buying share; and the fee pools — bancassurance, wealth, transaction banking — need scale this bank does not have [S0]. Its 14 branches buy relationships, not efficiency: cost-to-income is 58.6%, several points above what a bank of this size needs to earn its cost of capital [S6].

Five forces, briefly. Supplier power (depositors) is high and rising: the loan-to-deposit ratio of 1.0x means the bank must compete for every rupiah of funding [S0]. Buyer power (borrowers) is moderate: the SME borrower has alternatives, and the bank's 46.5% capital ratio is not a competitive weapon in a price negotiation. New entrants are a real threat at the small end, through digital banks and multifinance [S0]. Substitutes — securities, mutual funds, fintech lending — are growing but from a small base in Sumatra. Rivalry is intense and consolidating, which is precisely what the OJK's tier policy intends [S8]. The moat, on this evidence, is a local deposit franchise and a bank licence; neither is worth a premium multiple on its own.

Indonesian banking has historically been a licence-and-scale industry rather than a technology industry: the
binding constraints are capital, funding cost and supervisory standing, and the smallest banks have spent the
last decade being consolidated into larger groups. A regional bank in Sumatra typically funds itself from local
business deposits, lends to the same business community, and earns a margin that is wider than a large bank's but
carries higher credit and concentration risk. That structural position explains why the sector's small caps
trade at a discount to book in normal regimes and only re-rate on a control event.

The five-year record is one of a franchise shrinking in real terms. On the data pack's definition, net interest income fell from IDR1,018.0bn in FY2022 to IDR930.4bn in FY2025 while the loan book grew, which means the margin, not the volume, did the damage [S0]. The audited accounts put FY2025 net interest income at IDR909.3bn against IDR916.3bn in FY2024 [S6]; the pack allocates part of interest expense to a different line, so the two definitions differ while total operating income matches the audited accounts. The model's net interest income line follows the pack's definition [S0] — that is the series the engine forecasts from, and the assumptions file records the reconciliation. Non-interest income fell by more over the same period, from IDR93.5bn on the pack's basis [S0] to IDR59.4bn; the audited other operating income is IDR139.9bn in FY2024 falling to IDR76.8bn in FY2025 [S6], and the bank's own commentary attributes the drop to the collapse in recoveries of previously written-off loans [S6]. Operating expenses rose to IDR579.7bn from IDR535.1bn [S6], so pre-provision profit fell to IDR410.1bn [S0] and net profit to IDR320.0bn from IDR403.4bn [S6]. Return on equity fell to 6.1% and the bank's reported return on assets was 2.5% [S7]; the pack-derived ROA of 1.9% averages total assets rather than using the bank's own denominator, so we quote the reported ratio.

Two data points deserve care because they are easy to misread. First, the LK's allowance figure of IDR168.0bn is the stock of loan-loss allowance, not the annual charge: it is just below the stock of gross NPL of 1.6% on a IDR11,060.0bn book, and it rose by only about a tenth of itself during FY2025 [S6][S7]. Second, the operating-profit-to-PBT bridge in the audited accounts leaves no room for a large provision charge: operating profit was IDR406.4bn and PBT IDR409.6bn, so the net charge was effectively nil and the small positive residual is non-operating [S6][S0]. We therefore do not model the allowance balance as a cost. We model a through-cycle charge of 0.4% of average loans — above the FY2024 and FY2025 trough, because near-zero charges flatter the reported return on equity, but far below the allowance stock and below the gross NPL ratio, so coverage is roughly maintained as the book grows [S6][S7].

That charge is the lowest in the small-bank peer set and is the assumption most open to challenge. It is above this bank's own trough, where the allowance stock rose by only about a tenth of itself in FY2025 and the operating-profit-to-PBT bridge leaves no annual charge [S6], but it is below the through-cycle charges of the larger mortgage- and micro-heavy lenders in the peer set, whose books carry different loss histories and higher NPL stocks. Special-mention and restructured loans — which would locate the book between its reported NPL and its through-cycle charge, as the house bank screen requires — are not in any source we could archive, and we record that as an evidence gap rather than as evidence of a clean book [S7]. The sensitivity grid shows what a heavier charge does, read off the rendered table: a step up of six tenths of a percentage point at the base margin takes the twelve-month value from the middle of the three hundreds to just over three hundred a share, about a tenth, and a step down of the same size adds about the same. That is why the bear case carries the stress charge stacked with the margin and cost shocks rather than as a half-point trim [S0].

Our forecast reproduces the last actual year and then drifts only where there is a reason. Net interest income of IDR948.0bn holds the 5.6% margin on earning assets proxied by total assets (IDR17,195.5bn), which is where the FY2025 and H1-2026 run-rates sit [S0]. Non-interest income grows from the depressed base at 4.0% [S6]. Costs take cost-to-income to 60.0% in FY2026E — H1-2026 net profit ran below H1-2025 on flat net interest income as the Semarang branch and personnel costs ran ahead — then ease to 58.0% as the branch build is absorbed [S0][S7]. The result is net profit of IDR280.4bn, EPS Rp70 and ROE 5.1%; by FY2030E net profit is IDR365.1bn and ROE 5.6%.

The step down in FY2026E ROE is credit-cost normalisation, not a margin or cost haircut. The reported FY2025 return of 6.1% was earned with a provision charge near zero [S6]; applying the modelled 0.4% to the same book is what takes FY2026E ROE to 5.1%. NIM is held at the actual 5.6%, cost-to-income peaks at 60.0% in FY2026E and eases to 58.0%, and ROE then drifts up to 5.8% by the end of the horizon as the Semarang branch matures. Loans grow 3.6% in FY2026E — the FY2025 rate held rather than lifted, because the pack carries no June-2026 loan balance, total assets eased between March and June 2026, and first-half net profit was below the prior-year half [S0]. From FY2027E we lift growth to a mid-single-digit rate — our own inference from the KBMI II capital plan, which needs a growing book to compound retained earnings but states no lending target, not a management forecast [S8]. Non-interest income grows 4.0% from the collapsed base on fees and the wider branch network, not on a recoveries rebound, since no source points to one [S6][S7].

The capital path is the strategic constraint and it is comfortable. Equity rises from IDR5,450.8bn to IDR6,092.5bn by FY2028E on a 28.0% payout, which takes core capital through the IDR6.00tn threshold before management's end-2028 deadline without new shares [S8]. The modelled capital ratio stays near 46.4% against the reported 46.5% [S7], which tells you the bank is not capital-constrained in any ordinary sense: it is return-constrained, holding risk assets it cannot lend out at a spread that covers the cost of the equity behind them. That is why the loan-to-deposit ratio of 1.0x and the growth rate of 3.6% in FY2026E matter less than the margin and the cost line.

Cash generation and capital allocation follow from that. A bank's operating cash flow is not comparable across periods because deposit inflows dominate it, and the pack's own history shows the swing from a large outflow in FY2024 to an inflow in FY2025 [S0]; we do not read a signal into it. Dividends have been paid every year, falling from Rp34 to Rp22 a share as profit fell, a payout of 28.1% [S0]. There is no buyback programme in the model and no acquisition has been announced. The most recent share event in the archive is the resale of treasury shares announced in January 2025 — sold at an average Rp1,900 a share, bringing in cash without changing the share count [S2][S5] — and it predates the 30 June 2026 balance-sheet date; no share event since that date is disclosed in any source reviewed, which the post-balance-sheet review in the assumptions file records [S2][S0].

Earnings quality, run through the house screens. The provisioning trend is the flag, not the accruals ratio: a bank with a stable gross NPL and a near-zero charge is releasing rather than providing, and the FY2025 profit decline came when the recoveries that had been flattering non-interest income stopped [S6]. We treat the resulting 6.1% ROE as the top of the cycle, not the middle. On structure, the shares are not on the special monitoring board and carry no going-concern or late-filing notation in the sources reviewed; the concentration status is separate and is dealt with in section six [S9]. Related-party flows are an open evidence gap: the annual-report note that would quantify them is not in the archive, so we record "not established" rather than "none found", and the controlling shareholder relationship is the group fact we can verify [S0]. One limitation, stated plainly: the issuer's own site refused automated access, so the audited statements themselves are cited through the audited-accounts press summary and the exchange disclosure rather than as an archived PDF [S6][S8].

A bank is valued on its equity, so the method set is residual income, a justified price-to-book cross-check and a dividend discount model, weighted at the industry default of half justified P/B, three tenths residual income and two tenths DDM. That is the right set here because the balance sheet is the product: book value is observable, the return on it is the driver, and the dividend is the only cash the minority will ever see from a 28.0%-payout bank. An enterprise-value method would be meaningless on a deposit-funded balance sheet, and a pure earnings multiple would capitalise a trough.

The discount rate is built, not chosen, and we state where it sits against the house card. The engine takes the ten-year government yield of 7.4% less the sovereign default spread of 1.6%, plus a beta of 0.9 times the sum of the mature-market premium of 4.2% and the country risk premium of 2.5% [S0]. That build lands below both the sector's rate for the larger banks and the card's plain ten-year-yield-plus-IDR-premium floor, so we add a company premium of 0.6% and publish a cost of equity of 12.5% [S0]. We stop there: this is the smallest, least liquid and most concentrated bank in the set [S9], but the 30% liquidity haircut below already charges tradability, and a further single-name premium would double-count it. The sensitivity grid shows the value either side of the rate. There is no leverage in it because a bank is valued on the equity side, and the beta is the house industry default rather than a company regression — a real limitation for a stock that trades a few million rupiah a day.

The primary leg is the justified P/B. A sustainable ROE of 5.8% against a 12.5% cost of equity and terminal growth of 3.0% warrants 0.30 times book, which on the June-2026 book value per share the engine carries is Rp399 [S0]. One convention is disclosed rather than inherited: the engine's default sustainable ROE is the mean of the first three forecast years, when the Semarang branch build still depresses the return. We override it with the terminal ROE of 5.8%, because a warranted multiple is a steady-state formula; at the default convention the leg and therefore the weighted value would be lower. The residual income leg discounts the same economics year by year and lands at Rp220, -44.9% from the primary, because the terminal value of a negative spread is itself negative; the DDM lands at Rp256, -36.0% from the primary for the same reason. Both cross-checks are shown in the valuation table and both say the same thing: the franchise is worth well under its book. Weighted together they give Rp317 today and Rp337 in twelve months before the liquidity haircut [S0]. Note the two book numbers involved: Rp1,353 is the FY2025 year-end book the history carries, while the engine values on the June-2026 book, which is the balance-sheet date the pack uses.

Excess capital is the one thing that could make that value too low, and it is worth being explicit about why it is not in the base. Equity of IDR5,450.8bn against a reported CAR of 46.5% [S7] means the bank holds far more capital than its risk assets require; on a loan book of IDR11,060.0bn the regulatory floor is a fraction of that equity. The residual income and DDM legs do not ignore it — they charge every rupiah of equity at the cost of equity, which is exactly why a below-cost spread produces the negative residual income and terminal value above. What they assume is that the capital stays inside the bank. It has to until core capital clears the IDR6.00tn KBMI II threshold by management's end-2028 deadline [S8]; after that a special dividend or capital release would be worth more to shareholders than equity earning below its cost, while a buyback is the one route the free-float rule effectively rules out because the float is already short of the first deadline [S11]. No distribution or buyback has been announced [S2][S5][S8], and the controller has no evident need for cash. We therefore treat capital release as the main upside to fundamental value rather than a base-case input, and it is the first item in the signposts.

The cross-checks agree with each other and disagree with the market, which is the finding, not an accident. The stock trades at 1.45 times our FY2026E book and 29.2x our FY2026E earnings, with a dividend yield of 1.0% [S0]. Its own four-year trading history shows a book multiple above one times throughout, so the premium is not new; what is new is the regime that has begun to charge for concentrated ownership [S9][S11][S12]. The engine's reverse DCF cannot bracket today's price by moving the credit-cost path within any plausible range — there is no fundamental path that gets to the traded price — so we do not publish an implied value from it. The honest statement is that the price implies a return on equity several times what this balance sheet has earned or is likely to earn.

The sensitivity grid shows where the value is fragile and where it is not, and every sentence here is read off the rendered table rather than from a wider hypothetical range. Each axis steps by three tenths of a percentage point to a maximum of six tenths either way: at the base credit cost the margin steps move the twelve-month value from a little over three hundred to a little under three hundred and sixty a share, and at the base margin the credit-cost steps move it from the upper three hundreds down to just over three hundred. A full percentage point on the cost of equity, with terminal growth at the base, moves it from the high three hundreds to just under three hundred [S0]. None of those moves reaches the traded price, which is the point of the exercise.

Then the liquidity discount and the konglo lens. The shares trade IDR8.7m a day on average over three months [S0], more than an order of magnitude below the lowest band in the house liquidity table — the band whose floor is nine figures in rupiah and below which the full explicit haircut applies — and the house band table takes its full 30% haircut at that level. We apply it: the fundamental twelve-month value is Rp231 [S0]. At the lighter haircut some peers in the sector carry the fundamental would be higher, and we do not use it, because this ADTV sits far below the names that get the lighter band and the choice is the house maximum, not a name-specific judgement. For a konglo name the engine then takes the ratio of price to today's fundamental value — 9.4 times, a log gap of 2.24 — and keeps part of it for twelve months: the base regime case keeps 40% of the gap and gives Rp884, the bear regime case keeps 80% and still gives Rp361 because even a hostile regime does not close a tenfold gap in a year, and the bull regime case gives Rp2,417 [S0][S12]. The probability-weighted result is Rp1,137.

The compression shares are not symmetric and each is argued, not defaulted. The base keeps 40% and the bear closes 80%: the HSC status and the float deadline together are worth more compression than the deck's default, which is why the flags add to both [S9][S11]. The bull's -5% means the premium widens, which is what a float gap closed by a controller sell-down at the market price — rather than a discounted placement — would produce, and what an MSCI outcome short of Standalone would produce [S11][S12]. The bull carries 20% of the business weight and, because the gap is 9.4 times today's fundamental value, contributes most of the published target; that is a property of the lens rather than hidden bullishness, and the same lens produces the bear target of Rp361.

The lens carries two regime flags for this name: high-shareholding-concentration status, and the free-float step due inside the window, which together close more of the gap than the base deck would [S9][S11]. It is not a licence to skip the fundamental work: the fundamental value is what the lens is applied to. Today's fundamental value is Rp217 a share and the twelve-month fundamental — the leg the lens actually projects forward — is Rp231, against a price of Rp2,030 [S0]. Stated as a single sentence: the market is paying for scarcity and we expect scarcity to persist for part of the next year, which is why the target is well above fundamental value and still well below the price.

The largest downside risk to our call is that we are wrong about the regime, not about the bank. If the float stays at 9.1% and the concentration status is tolerated, the price can stay at 9.4 times today's fundamental value of Rp217 indefinitely, and the twelve-month target we publish is already generous to that possibility [S0][S9]. That is a risk to being short, and it is why the lens rather than the fundamental value sets the target.

Regulatory risk cuts both ways and is dated. The OJK's plan to remove the lowest KBMI tier forces either a capital raise or a merger by the end of 2028; the base case assumes retained earnings close a small gap, but a rights issue at a discount would dilute book value per share just as returns stay below the cost of equity [S8]. The consolidation path is real and we do not omit it: a bank of this size, with this capital and this deposit franchise, is the kind of asset a larger group would look at once the KBMI tier disappears [S8]. But it is not upside to the traded price. At 1.45 times our FY2026E book the market already pays Rp2,030 for a franchise whose warranted value is Rp337; an acquirer buying control at today's multiple would be paying far above what the returns justify, and the only way the path clears at or above the price is a strategic premium for the licence or the deposit base that no source evidences. We therefore carry it in the signposts, not in the base, and we would put a probability and a date on it the moment an approach is sourced. The free-float rule forces a controller sell-down or new shares to reach 12.5% by the end of March 2027 — a supply event that can compress the premium — with the full minimum due a year later [S11]. The MSCI consultation is the same story at index level: a freeze on increases is already in place, the feedback window closes at the end of April 2027 and the decision is due by the end of June 2027 [S12]. A Standalone reclassification would remove index demand permanently.

Macro and funding risk are the everyday version. The house macro deck has the policy rate flat and the rupiah under balance-of-payments pressure [S0]; for a bank funded entirely by domestic deposits with a loan-to-deposit ratio of 1.0x, a tight liquidity cycle raises the cost of funds before it slows the loan book. Every point of margin is worth roughly the same as a point of cost-to-income in the sensitivity grid, and the bank has little pricing power to defend either [S0][S6].

Credit risk is small in the reported numbers and large in the tail. Gross NPL is 1.6% and net 0.8%, with allowances just below the gross stock [S6][S7]; a regional SME book in one province is concentrated by borrower and by industry, and the FY2025 experience shows how much of the reported profit came from recoveries rather than from lending [S6]. Our 0.4% charge is above the recent actual precisely because the recent actual is not a through-cycle number. The bear case goes further than the base to a small-bank stress charge, and that is what makes it a genuine downside rather than a margin trim: the charge more than doubles, the margin narrows, lending slows and the cost base grows together. Even then it does not take net profit to zero — a stress charge on this loan book is a large slice of pre-provision profit, not all of it, and the coverage stock stands just below the gross NPL [S6][S7]. The bear is worth Rp249 against a base of Rp337.

Governance and liquidity risk are the konglo channels. A controller with more than nine tenths of the shares can set the dividend, choose the capital route and time any sell-down; a float of 9.1% means the exit is the market's problem. The traded value is below the fund's liquidity floor, which is why the valuation carries the explicit haircut rather than a hidden rate premium [S0].

Business scenarios, then regime scenarios — they are separate and must not be confused. The business cases shock the same four drivers in mirrored directions: credit cost, NIM, loan growth and cost-to-income, with probabilities of 50% base, 30% bear and 20% bull. The base is the last actual re-priced, not a cautious path: it keeps the actual NIM, the FY2025 growth rate and a cost ratio that peaks in FY2026E and falls thereafter, and its lower return than FY2025 is the credit charge, as section three sets out. The credit-cost shocks are deliberately not mirrored in magnitude, because the bank's charge is already at its floor and a stress can add far more than a recovery can subtract; the assumptions file records that reason against the symmetry check. The bear case — a tighter margin, the stress charge, slower lending and a heavier cost base — is worth Rp249; the base Rp337; the bull case, where the margin holds and the branch build is absorbed faster, Rp435. The regime cases sit around them and produce the published target.

Signposts that would change our view. Upward: a real deposit-cost easing that lifts the margin by more than the cost line grows; a special dividend or capital release once core capital clears the KBMI II threshold, which would move fundamental value toward book and is the main upside to the fundamental leg (section four); a control or consolidation transaction, which we would treat as a dated event with a probability the moment it is sourced, although at today's multiple an acquirer would be paying far above warranted value; or evidence that the exchange will tolerate the current float beyond the deadlines. Downward: a discounted rights issue, a controller sell-down that hits the market at once, an MSCI Standalone decision, or a credit charge that normalises faster than we model.

Ownership is the defining governance fact. The controlling shareholder is PT Mestika Benua Mas, and the shareholder register shows the great majority of the shares held by insiders, with a free float of 9.1% [S0]. The exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, which had 82 issuers on it as of 22 October 2026, includes Bank Mestika [S9]. Membership is a concentrated-ownership disclosure status with index consequences — exclusion from the IHSG calculation and from the main liquidity indices — and is not by itself a finding of wrongdoing; we treat it as a structural fact about who sets the price [S9]. No enforcement action, index deletion on governance grounds or change-of-control process appears in the sources reviewed [S9][S12].

The free-float rule turns that structure into a dated obligation. With a float below the intermediate threshold and a market capitalisation above the large-cap line, the bank must reach 12.5% by 31 March 2027 and the full minimum by 31 March 2028, a gap of 3.4% and 4.6 months to the first deadline [S11][S0]. There are three routes, not two. The controller can sell, which puts supply into a market that trades a few million rupiah a day; the company can issue shares, which dilutes book just as returns sit below the cost of equity; or the bank can transfer the treasury stock it already owns, which adds no dilution. That third route is live and sized: the bank announced a plan to transfer 63.02 million treasury shares from the April-June 2020 buyback in September 2024, with Ciptadana Sekuritas as arranger [S5], and after the January-2025 resale tranche 60.97 million shares remained [S2]. Sold into the market, that stock would lift the float from 9.1% to a little over ten and a half per cent — closing a little under half of the 3.4% gap and still leaving the bank short of the 12.5% step. No timetable for the remainder is disclosed in the sources reviewed: the arranger and the working-capital use of proceeds are stated, and the January-2025 tranche was sold at an average of Rp1,900 a share against an average Rp1,095 buyback cost in 2020, which the company reported as a disposal without loss — the discount into this market is a liquidity discount, not a price discount — but there is no completion schedule [S5][S2]. The unsold balance is therefore both the cleanest part of the float solution and a supply overhang into the thinnest market in the book, and it is the reason the premium compression we model is dated rather than immediate. Supply events of any of the three kinds are value-relevant and none is under minority control.

Related-party dealings are an open evidence gap, not a clean bill. For a bank controlled by a single family group, related-party lending, deposits and guarantees are the modal value-destruction channel, and the FY2025 annual report's related-party note is the one document that would quantify them as a share of the book. It is not in the archived sources: the issuer's site refused automated access and no press summary carries the note [S6]. We therefore record "not established — checked" rather than "none found", treat the absence as a limitation on the fundamental value, and will close it at the next refresh before relying on the valuation for any action. Pledged shares: no pledge disclosure was found in the sources reviewed, so we record "none found — checked" rather than assert there is none. Auditor and opinion: the FY2025 figures we cite are described as audited, but the audit report itself was not machine-readable from the issuer's site and is therefore not quoted here [S6]. The dividend record is continuous and, at Rp22 a share against Rp79 of earnings, a 28.1% payout [S0].

Board and management: the president director is Achmad Suherman Kartasasmita, who fronted both the FY2025 results briefing and the exchange answer on KBMI II [S7][S8]. There is no independent chairman disclosure in the sources we could archive, and we do not infer one. ESG exposures specific to this name are the social and governance side rather than the environmental side: a regional lender's environmental footprint is small, while its concentration, minority representation and the treatment of the free-float deadline are the material issues. No sustainability report was reachable for review; we flag that as an evidence gap rather than a clean bill.

The dated events that matter are regulatory and index-driven, in this order: the free-float step to 12.5% by 31 March 2027 [S11]; the close of MSCI's consultation feedback on 30 April 2027 and its decision by 30 June 2027 [S12]; the final free-float deadline on 31 March 2028 [S11]; and management's target of reaching the KBMI II core-capital threshold before the end of 2028 [S8]. The FY2026 results, expected in the first quarter of 2027, are the first hard test of whether the cost build is being absorbed.

Between updates we monitor six things: net interest margin and cost of funds against the flat policy-rate path [S0]; cost-to-income, where the Semarang branch is the swing factor [S7]; the credit charge and the allowance cover against gross NPL [S6]; the loan-to-deposit ratio, because a bank at 1.0x has no funding slack [S0]; core capital against the IDR6.00tn threshold [S8]; and the free float itself, since a step toward the regulatory minimum is the single most likely trigger for the premium to compress [S11]. We would revisit the rating on a sourced control transaction, on a margin recovery that survives two quarters, or on a rights issue priced at a discount to book.

bear.narrative: Funding competition in Sumatra compresses the margin, personnel and branch costs stay elevated, and slower loan growth leaves the bank with even more excess capital earning below its cost; OJK's removal of KBMI 1 then forces a discounted rights issue that dilutes book value per share just as returns stay below the cost of equity.

bull.narrative: Deposit competition eases with the BI rate path, the margin holds, branch and personnel costs are absorbed faster, and lending accelerates toward the KBMI 2 plan, so ROE recovers toward its pre-2024 level without issuing equity.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs NIM and credit cost
12-month value vs cost of equity and terminal growth

adjustments.why: on the exchange's HSC list (as of 2026-10-22): out of the IHSG, the LQ45/IDX30/IDX80 and the MSCI indexes [konglo deck S3]
free float 9.07% must reach 12.5% by 2027-03-31 — controller sell-down or new shares inside the window [konglo deck S25]

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: FY2025 gross loans grew 3.65% (Rp10.83trn to Rp11.23trn [S7]; the data pack carries Rp11.06trn on a slightly narrower definition [S0]). FY2026E holds that 3.65%: the H1-2026 balance sheet did not accelerate (total assets eased from Rp16.41trn in March to Rp16.21trn in June [S0]), net profit fell year on year in the half [S0], and no source shows lending accelerating before the KBMI 2 plan. The step-up to 5-6% from FY2027E is our inference from that plan rather than management guidance: the exchange answer states the KBMI 2 target and the retained-earnings route but no lending target, and a 5-6% book is what growing earning assets while core capital compounds toward the Rp6trn threshold by end-2028 requires [S8].

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: FY2025 DPK grew 6.8% (Rp10.29trn to Rp10.99trn [S6]); deposits are already 100.6% of loans, so funding must lead lending. Growth of 5-6% is held slightly above loan growth to keep the loan-to- deposit ratio below 100% and protects the margin against a repeat of the 2025 deposit competition in Sumatra described in the results commentary [S6].

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: Earning assets are proxied by total assets: the non-loan 34% of the balance sheet is almost entirely government securities, placements and Bank Indonesia balances, and fixed assets are only ~4% of the total. FY2025 total assets Rp16.66trn against loans Rp11.06trn gives 1.51x [S6, S0]; held at 1.50x because growth is funded by deposits rather than by adding low-yielding securities.

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: On the earning-asset proxy, FY2025 NII was 5.60% (data pack NII Rp930.4bn on average earning assets of Rp16.62trn [S0]) and H1-2026 NII of Rp462.9bn annualises to 5.67% on average assets of Rp16.31trn [S0]. FY2026E is set at 5.60%, the actual run-rate, and held flat: the 2026 BI rate path in the house macro deck is flat at 5.75% and there is no sourced reason for either a squeeze or a recovery. The LK's own NII of Rp909.33bn [S6] differs from the pack only because the pack allocates Rp21bn of interest expense to a different line; total operating income matches within 0.4% [S6, S0].

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: Non-interest income fell in FY2025 because recoveries of written-off loans collapsed (the LK puts other operating income at Rp76.85bn against Rp139.86bn [S6]). FY2026E grows 4% from the pack's lower base on fees and bancassurance, not on a recovery rebound; the 5% used from FY2027E reflects a branch network being built out (14 branches, 39 sub-branches [S7]).

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: FY2025 cost-to-income was 58.6% on the pack's total operating income and opex (Rp579.73bn opex on Rp986.2bn of LK operating income, 58.8% [S6]). FY2026E rises to 60%: H1-2026 net profit of Rp118.9bn is 14% below H1-2025 on flat NII [S0] as personnel cost (Rp324.71bn in FY2025 [S6]) and the 2025 Semarang branch [S7] run ahead of revenue. The branch build is then absorbed, taking CTI to 58% by FY2030E - still above the FY2024 level.

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: The LK's Rp168.01bn CKPN figure is the allowance balance, not the annual charge: it equals ~97% of gross NPL (1.56% of Rp11.2trn loans [S7]) and rose only Rp19.0bn in FY2025 [S6], and the operating- profit-to-PBT bridge in the audited accounts (operating profit Rp406.45bn against PBT of Rp409.6bn [S6, S0]) leaves no room for a Rp168bn charge. The P&L charge was therefore near zero in FY2024-25. We model 0.40% - above that trough because the allowance rose Rp19.0bn (0.17% of average loans) and because near-zero charges flatter the 2025 ROE - but far below the allowance balance and below the 1.56% gross NPL: coverage stays at ~97% while the book grows.

assumptions.label: Other items
assumptions.basis: The historical residual is pbt minus operating profit: Rp3.11bn in FY2025 (PBT Rp409.56bn against operating profit Rp406.45bn [S6, S0]) and Rp0.24bn in FY2024. Immaterial and not recurring, so the forecast carries zero.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 effective rate is 21.87% (tax Rp89.57bn on PBT Rp409.56bn [S0]), below the 22% statutory rate in Law 7/2021 and consistent with FY2024 (22.6%); the FY2025 rate is held.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: no minorities on the consolidated income statement in the data pack [S0]

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 DPS of Rp22.33 on EPS Rp79.42 is a 28% payout, down from Rp34.25 in FY2024 (34%), because profit fell and the bank is retaining capital to reach the Rp6trn KBMI 2 threshold before end-2028 [S8]. The 28% actual ratio is held across the forecast: it already retains enough (with net profit of ~Rp280bn a year and a 46.49% CAR [S7]) to reach the Rp6trn core-capital threshold before end-2028, and holding the last actual avoids an unsourced payout drift in either direction. BBMD has paid a dividend every year; the June 2026 payment (Rp22.33 a share) is in the pack [S0].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No new shares in the base case: the capital gap to KBMI 2 is closed from retained earnings at a CAR of 46.49% [S7, S8]. The most recent share event in the archive is the resale of 2.0558m treasury shares announced on 7 January 2025 (Rp1.89bn at an average Rp1,900), which predates the 30 June 2026 balance-sheet date by seventeen months and does not change the share count [S2, S5]; no share event since 30 June 2026 is disclosed in any archived source, so the count is held flat.

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: Reported CAR of 46.49% at December 2025 on equity of Rp5.45trn [S7] implies RWA of ~Rp11.72trn, i.e. 1.06x gross loans - the bank's non-loan assets are largely zero-risk-weighted government securities. 1.06x is used, so the modelled capital ratio reflects the disclosed one rather than a guess.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: Cap test per VAL_BANKS item 5: g <= ROE x (1 - payout). The model's FY2030E ROE is ~5.4% on a 30% payout, a 3.8% cap; 3.0% is set inside it and slightly below long-run IDR nominal growth because a bank that already holds 46% CAR cannot compound its book faster than its equity allows.

challenges.challenge: Section 3 cites [S6] for FY2022/FY2025 NII of Rp1,018.0bn/Rp930.4bn and non-interest income of Rp93.5bn/Rp59.4bn, but S6 actually reports NII of Rp916.27bn/Rp909.33bn and other operating income of Rp139.86bn/Rp76.85bn (packet F7-F10). The cited numbers are S0 data-pack definitions, not S6, and differ from the audited figures by up to 26%. ROA is also stated as 1.9% against the report fact F23 of 2.49%.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now cites [S0] for the pack-definition NII/NOII series and gives the audited S6 pair (Rp909.33bn/Rp916.27bn and Rp76.85bn/Rp139.86bn) alongside, states that the model NII line follows the pack definition with the reconciliation in the assumptions, and quotes the reported ROA of 2.49% from S7 rather than the pack-derived ratio.

challenges.challenge: The primary justified-P/B leg uses roe_sustainable 5.1809%, which is the engine mean of FY2026-28 forecast ROE, not a sustainable ROE; the model own FY2035E terminal ROE is 5.84%. Section 4 presents it as a sustainable ROE of 5.2% without disclosing the convention. At 5.84% the warranted P/B is 0.314x and the leg is ~Rp424, not Rp327.
challenges.answer: Added valuation.roe_sustainable 0.0584 (the model terminal FY2035E ROE) with a note, and section 4 now discloses the engine default convention and says the leg and weighted value would be lower without the override; the primary leg is Rp426 at 0.32x book.

challenges.challenge: The bank reports 46.5% CAR (RWA ~Rp11.7trn against equity Rp5.45trn) and the report itself says it cannot lend out the equity at a spread covering COE; yet the residual-income terminal assumes perpetual 3% book growth at a negative spread (pv_ri -Rp2,394bn, pv_tv -Rp1,919bn) and values the equity at 0.155x book. No scenario or bridge values a special dividend, buyback or capital release after the KBMI II threshold.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the 0.155x figure is post-haircut, quantifies equity against the reported CAR and loan book, explains that the RI and DDM legs already charge all equity at COE, and justifies why release is not in the base: core capital must clear the KBMI II threshold by end-2028, no distribution is announced, and a buyback conflicts with the free-float rule. Capital release is named the main fundamental upside and first signpost.

challenges.challenge: The OJK removal of KBMI 1 is a sourced catalyst forcing consolidation or a capital raise [S8], but the report assigns zero probability to a control or merger transaction (cannot source) and the bull case shocks only credit cost, NIM, loan growth and CTI. At 1.5x book a takeover is unattractive, but the report should say so rather than omit the path.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now carries the consolidation path explicitly: OJK's KBMI 1 removal is a dated end-2028 catalyst, but at the traded multiple an acquirer would pay far above warranted value, so the path clears below the price absent a sourced strategic premium; it stays in the signposts with a probability to be set when an approach is sourced.

challenges.challenge: For a 91%-controlled konglo bank, related-party lending and group flows are the modal value-destruction channel (EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS #4, konglo card section 3), but section 6 records only that they are not disclosed in the sources reviewed. The FY2025 annual-report related-party note is not in the source list; a press summary cannot establish absence.
challenges.answer: Recorded as an open evidence gap rather than absence in sections 3 and 6: the FY2025 annual-report related-party note is not archived, the issuer site refused automated access, so we state not established and treat it as a limitation on fundamental value to close at refresh.

challenges.challenge: The bear case lifts the credit charge only to 0.7% (base 0.4% + 30bp) for a one-province Sumatra SME book with 1.56% gross NPL and 97% allowance cover. Peer through-cycle charges run 1.5-2.1% (BJTM 1.5%, BBTN 1.7%, BDMN 2.1%); a genuine stress would take net profit toward zero and the bear value well below Rp122.
challenges.answer: Bear credit-cost shock raised to a small-bank stress charge (base 0.4% plus 0.6pp), and the asymmetry against the bull is justified in qc_justifications: the actual charge is at its floor, so a stress can add more than a recovery can subtract. Section 5 now argues the resulting bear value rather than calling it a margin trim.

challenges.challenge: The base case never recovers: ROE 5.06% FY2026E rising only to 5.84% by 2035, below the 6.07% FY2025 actual and the 8.1%/8.8% of FY2024/23, while cost-to-income is lifted to 60% (actual 58.6%) and non-interest income grows 4% from a collapsed base with no recovery rebound. The MOST_LIKELY_BASE_CASE card says caution belongs in the bear case, which already exists at Rp122.
challenges.answer: The FY2026E step-down is not a cautious stack: FY2025's 6.10% ROE was earned with a near-zero charge [S6], so the modelled 0.4% charge on the same book is precisely why FY2026E ROE is 5.06%; NIM is the actual, CTI peaks then falls, and ROE drifts to the 5.84% terminal. Section 3 now says this and the no-recovery claim is answered with the re-pricing arithmetic.

challenges.challenge: The 4.0% FY2026E loan growth (above the 3.65% actual) is justified by the H1-2026 balance sheet still growing (total assets Rp16.41trn in March to Rp16.21trn in June, [S0]), but the cited numbers show a 1.2% decline and the June loan balance is not given.
challenges.answer: FY2026E loan growth cut to the FY2025 actual 3.65%; the H1-2026 characterisation is corrected (total assets eased from March to June), the pack carries no June loan balance and that is said, first-half profit was below the prior-year half.

challenges.challenge: The 0.4% through-cycle credit charge is the lowest in the BANKS peer set (BINA 0.65%, BNII 0.8%, BBNI 1.08%, BJTM 1.5%, BBTN 1.7%, BDMN 2.1%) for a 1.56%-NPL regional SME book. Section 3 argues it is above the bank near-zero trough but never that 0.4% is a full-cycle rate; special-mention and restructured loans, required by VAL_BANKS #4, are absent.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now defends 0.4% against the bank's own loss history and says it is the lowest in the peer set and the assumption most open to challenge; special-mention and restructured loans are recorded as an evidence gap, not a clean bill, and the sensitivity implication is stated.

challenges.challenge: COE 11.85% is built as (7.4%-1.6%) + 0.9x(4.2%+2.5%), not the VAL_BANKS card 10y yield + IDR ERP 5.0-6.0% (7.4%+5.0-6.0% = 12.4-13.4%), and sits below BBCA/BDMN/BNGA at 12.45% for the smallest, least liquid, most concentrated name in the set. The 1.6pp sovereign-spread subtraction and beta-on-ERP are unexplained, and no deposit-beta/CASA path is given.
challenges.answer: COE reconciled to the VAL_BANKS card: a 0.60pp single-name premium takes the engine build from 11.85% to 12.45%, the sector rate and card floor. Section 4 explains the build, the premium and why no further premium is added (the 30% liquidity haircut already charges tradability); the sensitivity grid shows the value either side. The 13.4% end is beyond the fixed grid and is argued, not tabulated.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says the fundamental value is Rp199 a share while the summary and QC say Rp210. The engine v_fundamental (199.46) is today value and tp_fundamental (209.74) is the 12-month base, but the text uses both to describe the fundamental. Section 4 also multiplies 0.25 by BVPS Rp1,353 to reach Rp327, while the engine uses the June-2026 BVPS Rp1,329 (0.2464x).
challenges.answer: Section 4 now distinguishes today's fundamental value from the twelve-month fundamental the lens projects, and states that the engine values on the June-2026 book while Rp1,352.8 is the FY2025 year-end book the history carries.

challenges.challenge: The bull regime case (25% probability) produces Rp2,397, above the Rp2,030 price (premium kept 105% of a 10.2x gap), and contributes 54% of the Rp1,105 target, yet section 4 and section 5 do not argue why the premium widens for this name. The base 40% is the deck default (30% + HSC 5% + float 5%).
challenges.answer: Section 4 now argues each compression share: base 40% and bear 80% from the HSC and float flags, bull -10% from a float gap closed by a market-price sell-down rather than a discounted placement. It also discloses that the bull contributes most of the target because the gap is 9.4x, and shows the same lens producing the bear target.

challenges.challenge: The 30% liquidity discount is called the house explicit 30% haircut with no cited band table or ADTV comparison. BBMD ADTV is Rp8.7m/day; peers use 0% (BINA, BDMN, BNGA, BBTN), 20% (BSIM, BTPN, BNII) and 30% (BSWD, ADTV Rp69.7m), so the choice is the house maximum and should be shown.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now quotes the three-month ADTV from the pack explicitly, says the name sits below the fund's lowest liquidity band and that the house band table takes its full 30% haircut there, and that lighter peer bands are not used because this ADTV is far below them.

challenges.challenge: Section 6 states the January-2025 resale was 'repriced below the 2020 cost' [S5][S2]; S2 gives an average resale price of Rp1,900 with 'tanpa kerugian' and S5 gives the 2020 buyback cost as Rp1,095, i.e. a resale ~73% above cost. An inverted sourced fact that manufactures a distress signal for the supply-overhang argument.
challenges.answer: Section 6 now restates the January-2025 tranche from the two primary disclosures: the shares were sold at an average of Rp1,900 against an average Rp1,095 buyback cost in 2020, reported by the company as a disposal without loss, so the discount into this market is a liquidity discount and not a price discount; the supply-overhang argument is kept unchanged because it never depended on the price direction, and both figures are now facts F39 (S2) and F40 (S5) rather than prose.

challenges.challenge: Section 3 and the share_change basis call the ~1m-share treasury resale 'the only capital action since the balance-sheet date', but S2 is dated 7 January 2025, seventeen months before the 30 June 2026 balance-sheet date, and no later share event is in any archived source.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now dates the treasury resale to the January-2025 announcement and says it predates the 30 June 2026 balance-sheet date, with no share event since that date disclosed in any source reviewed [S2][S0]; the share_change basis carries the same correction and valuation.post_bs_review states explicitly that no share issue, buyback, split, treasury resale or dividend-in-shares has occurred since 30 June 2026, so valuation.bridge stays empty for share events as well as asset events.

challenges.challenge: The section 3 and section 4 sensitivity prose contradicts the rendered grid: 'Moving NIM three percentage points ... middle of the low hundreds to middle of the high hundreds' against a +/-0.6pp grid spanning 313.8-360.0 at base credit cost, and 'a half-point step-up in credit cost removes roughly a third to half' against a 337-to-300 (about 11%) move at +0.6pp. This overstatement is load-bearing for the 'no plausible path reaches the price' conclusion.
challenges.answer: Both sensitivity sentences are rewritten off the rendered grid and no longer claim a three-point NIM range or a one-third-to-half credit-cost hit: the text states that each axis steps three tenths of a point to a maximum of six tenths, that the margin steps span a little over three hundred to a little under three hundred and sixty at base credit cost, that the credit-cost steps run from the upper three hundreds down to just over three hundred at base margin, and that a full point on the cost of equity takes it from the high three hundreds to just under three hundred [S0]. The figures are worded rather than typed because the house rule bans typed numbers; the rendered table in the same section carries the exact cells. '29.2x times' is now '29.2x our FY2026E earnings' and 'an 12.5% cost of equity' is now 'a 12.5% cost of equity' in the summary and section 4.

missing_bull_case.note: The cases omit the largest balance-sheet lever: 46.5% CAR (RWA ~Rp11.7trn vs equity Rp5.45trn, ~2x a 20% target) could be distributed after the KBMI II threshold in 2028; the RI/DDM legs instead trap it in a negative-spread perpetual terminal. Bull also omits the OJK-forced consolidation path.

missing_bear_case.note: Related-party lending and group flows are not quantified for a 91%-controlled konglo bank (annual-report note unread); the bear credit charge of 0.7% is far below the 1.5-2.1% that small-bank peers run (BJTM, BBTN, BDMN) for a 1.56%-NPL Sumatra SME book; deposit-mix/beta stress is absent.

assumption_realism.note: Base ROE never recovers (5.06% FY2026E, 5.84% terminal) versus 6.07% actual and 8.1-8.8% in FY2023-24; cti 60%, credit cost 0.4% and noii +4% all stack cautious. The 4% loan-growth basis calls a Rp16.41trn-to-Rp16.21trn asset decline still growing. No deposit beta or CASA/TD path despite LDR ~1.0x.

bias.note: Re-audited from the last actual, not from the prior QC note. The base keeps every anchor the card names: NIM 5.60% = the FY2025 run-rate (NII 930.44 on average earning assets 16,615 [S0]); FY2026E loan growth 3.65% = the FY2025 actual [S6][S7]; payout 28.12% and tax 21.87% = actuals [S0]; terminal g 3.0% inside the ROE x (1 - payout) cap of 4.2%. The departures are offsetting, not stacked. Downward: credit cost 0.40% against a ~nil actual (45.05bn FY2026E charge) and CTI 60.0% against 58.6% [S6][S7], both sourced (operating profit 406.45 against PBT 409.56, allowance +Rp19.0bn = 0.17% of average loans; H1-2026 profit -14% YoY [S0]) and both disclosed in section 3. Upward: loan growth steps to 5% from FY2027E on the KBMI II plan that states no lending target [S8]; the justified-P/B leg overrides the engine default sustainable ROE 5.18% upward to the 5.84% terminal at 50% weight; and COE 12.45% sits exactly on the VAL_BANKS floor (7.45% 10y + 5.0% ERP) rather than mid-band. Scenarios mirror NIM +/-0.4pp, growth +/-2pp and CTI +/-3pp exactly; the one asymmetry (credit cost +0.6pp bear against -0.3pp bull) is sourced to the charge floor and stated in section 5. The -1.02pp FY2025A-to-FY2026E ROE calibration gap is the credit charge and is disclosed in section 3. Net: neither a default haircut nor a cautious stack - the SELL is the price-versus- fundamental gap of the konglo lens, not a bearish base; if anything the fundamental is generous (COE at the band floor, terminal ROE override at half weight).

Section 4 introduces "today's fundamental value Rp217" in the sentence after quoting "Rp317 today and Rp337 in twelve months before the liquidity haircut".
